records.notes: Cohort record. The 36 Hill labourers who signed five-year contracts on 10 September 1834 with George Charles Arbuthnot of Hunter-Arbuthnot & Co., and arrived in Mauritius aboard the Atlas on 2 November 1834 after a six-week voyage. They were the very first indentured Indians under the new system, recorded at what is now the Aapravasi Ghat UNESCO World Heritage Site.

source.title: Some New Information — 2nd November 1834: The Arrival of the Pioneer Indentured Labourers in Mauritius

records.notes: Pioneer cohort record. The Whitby (249 indentureds on board) and Hesperus arrived together at Berbice with 396 total Indian indentured workers — the very first to British Guiana. Voyage 112 days, 5 deaths en route. The arrival is now commemorated as Indian Arrival Day in Guyana (5 May). Backed by sugar-plantation owner John Gladstone in what was known as the 'Gladstone Experiment'.

source.title: The Whitby and Hesperus: The First Indian Indentured Servant Ships to Guyana
source.publisher: West Indian Diplomacy / Guyana National Trust / Royal Historical Society

descendants_named: Sewdass Sadhu (son, b. 1 Jan 1903 in Benares — sugar worker at Waterloo Estates; built the Waterloo 'Temple in the Sea' single-handedly over 25 years after the colonial government demolished his first onshore temple in 1947)
Two younger sons (names not in public record)
records.notes: Indentured Hindu couple from Benares who carried their infant son Sewdass (b. 1 Jan 1903) and his two younger brothers to Trinidad. The family lived at Brickfield and worked the Waterloo sugar plantation. Sewdass's lifelong project — moving rocks by bicycle into the Gulf of Paria after work — became the Sewdass Sadhu Shiv Mandir, now a national monument completed by the government in 1995 on the 150th anniversary of Indian Arrival.

source.title: Sewdass Sadhu Shiv Mandir — National Library and Information System (NALIS), Trinidad

destination.estate: Indentured to a powerful European employer in Durban (name redacted in Gandhi's account)

records.notes: The Tamil indentured labourer whose 1894 case changed the course of Mahatma Gandhi's life. Beaten so severely by his European master that two of his teeth were broken, he fell at the young advocate Gandhi's feet and pleaded for rescue. Gandhi got his indenture transferred to another employer and prosecuted the master — the case that won Gandhi his standing among indentured Indians in Natal and seeded what would become satyagraha. Documented by Gandhi himself in *An Autobiography* (Chapter 44).

source.title: An Autobiography or The Story of My Experiments with Truth — Chapter 44: Balasundaram
source.publisher: M. K. Gandhi (1927) — via Gandhi Ashram Sevagram

Chandrikapersad 'Chan' Santokhi (great-grandson, b. 3 Feb 1959 Lelydorp — youngest of nine, 9th President of Suriname 2020–2025, took oath in Sanskrit)
records.notes: An unusually well-documented multi-district lineage. Chan Santokhi has publicly stated that his great-grandparents on both sides came from five distinct Indian districts: Ghazipur and Azamgarh in eastern Uttar Pradesh; Chhapra (Saran district) and Mau in Bihar; and Bharatpur in Rajasthan. They were brought to Suriname as indentured labourers in the 19th century. Santokhi's swearing-in as Suriname's President in Sanskrit (July 2020) was a first.

destination.estate: Réunion sugar industry — earliest indentured intake

records.notes: Pioneer cohort record. La Turquoise carried 15 Telugu-speaking workers from the French enclave of Yanaon to Île Bourbon (Réunion) in April 1828 — six years before the British 'Atlas' brought 36 Hill Dhangars to Mauritius. The earliest documented intake of Indian indentured labour anywhere in the European colonial world. Subsequent voyages 1828–1830 came from Yanaon, 1848–1860 from Pondicherry and Karikal, and 1860–1885 from British Calcutta + Madras.

source.title: Indentured labour from India in 19th-century Reunion Island
source.publisher: Portail des Mémoires de l'Esclavage à La Réunion / Le Mauricien

descendants_named: Dookie Meah's descendants (founder of Trinidad's first mosque)
records.notes: Pioneer cohort record. The Fatel Razack — owned by Indian Muslim trader Ibrahim bin Yusuf — departed Calcutta on 16 February 1845 and reached the Gulf of Paria on 30 May 1845 (Indian Arrival Day in Trinidad & Tobago). 227 boarded, 6 died en route, 2 infants born on board — 225 disembarked. Among them: Dookie Meah, listed as passenger #4 on the register, who went on to found Trinidad's first mosque.

source.title: Fatel Razack — Wikipedia / National Trust of Trinidad & Tobago
source.publisher: Wikipedia / National Trust T&T / Madras Courier / Trinidad Express

records.notes: Pioneer cohort record. The SS Blundell arrived at Old Harbour Bay, Jamaica on 10 May 1845 — just 20 days before the Fatel Razack reached Trinidad — carrying 261 Indian indentured workers from Calcutta. Their arrival began Jamaica's indentured intake of 37,027 Indians over the next 72 years (1845–1916). The Jamaica Indentureship Collection 1845–1958 is now part of UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

source.title: SS Blundell — Jamaica's First Indian Indentured Servant Ship
source.publisher: West Indian Diplomacy / UNESCO Memory of the World / Jamaica Timeline

Sundarlal Popo Bahora ('Sundar Popo', grandson, 4 Nov 1943 – 2 May 2000, Barrackpore — Father of Chutney Music; his 1969 hit *Nana and Nani*, which immortalised his Girmitiya grandparents' drinking habits, is the foundational record of the chutney genre and indirectly inspired Lord Kitchener and chutney-soca artists)
Chandra Sundar (granddaughter — continuing the singing tradition)
records.notes: An entire musical genre, *chutney*, was founded on the memory of these unnamed grandparents. Sundar Popo's 1969 song *Nana and Nani* — about a Girmitiya couple's drinking habits — became the foundational record of Indo-Caribbean chutney music, fusing Bhojpuri folk with Caribbean rhythms. Their grandson is honoured by the Sundarlal Popo Bahora Auditorium at the Southern Academy for the Performing Arts in San Fernando, Trinidad.

source.title: Sundar Popo (Wikipedia / EasternEye / Better India)
